Juniors can start rowing from the age of 12.

The season starts in April, when the ice has gone.

Only after passing the sculling test.

The duty officer decides whether boats may go out.

We enter three regattas each summer.

Book in the app at least one hour ahead.

Parking is free behind the boathouse.

Yes, we hold a spring party and an autumn dinner.

Email the treasurer before 1 December.

You can pause for one season at a time.

A board elected at the annual meeting in March.

Sign up for a work day on the club calendar.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

Markup is not text. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

# Vanliga frågor

### Hur blir jag medlem?

Fyll i formuläret på medlemssidan.

### Behöver jag kunna simma?

Ja, alla medlemmar måste kunna simma 200 meter.

### Finns det en åldersgräns?

Juniorer kan börja ro från 12 års ålder.

### När börjar säsongen?

Säsongen börjar i april, när isen har gått.

### Kan jag prova innan jag går med?

Ja, vi har prova-på-kvällar varje tisdag i maj.

### Vad ska jag ha på mig?

Åtsittande träningskläder som du kan röra dig i.

### Får jag en nyckel till båthuset?

Ja, depositionen för nyckeln är 100 kr.

### Får jag ta med en gäst?

Gäster får ro två gånger per säsong tillsammans med en medlem.

### Ingår träning med tränare?

Träning med tränare på tisdagar och torsdagar ingår i avgiften.

### Får jag ro ensam?

Först när du har klarat singelprovet.

### Vad händer vid dåligt väder?

Dagens ansvarige bestämmer om båtarna får gå ut.

### Tävlar ni?

Vi deltar i tre regattor varje sommar.

### Finns det ett gym?

Ja, gymmet är öppet året runt.

### Kan jag hyra en båt?

Båtarna är bara för medlemmar och kan inte hyras.

### Hur bokar jag en båt?

Boka i appen minst en timme i förväg.

### Finns det duschar?

Ja, det finns duschar och bastu i klubbhuset.

### Kan jag förvara min egen båt?

Privata båtar kan förvaras mot en avgift om det finns plats.

### Finns det skåp?

Ja, ett skåp kostar 100 kr per säsong.

### Finns det parkering?

Parkeringen bakom båthuset är gratis.

### Ordnar ni sociala aktiviteter?

Ja, vi har en vårfest och en höstmiddag.

### Hur säger jag upp mitt medlemskap?

Mejla kassören före den 1 december.

### Kan jag pausa mitt medlemskap?

Du kan pausa en säsong i taget.

### Vem driver klubben?

En styrelse som väljs på årsmötet i mars.

### Hur kan jag hjälpa till?

Anmäl dig till en arbetsdag i klubbkalendern.

### Hur blir jag medlem?

Fyll i formuläret på medlemssidan.

### Behöver jag kunna simma?

Ja, alla medlemmar måste kunna simma 200 meter.

Juniorer kan börja ro från 12 års ålder.

### När börjar säsongen?

Säsongen börjar i april, när isen har gått.

Ja, vi har prova-på-kvällar varje tisdag i maj.

### Vad ska jag ha på mig?

Åtsittande träningskläder som du kan röra dig i.

Ja, depositionen för nyckeln är 100 kr.

Gäster får ro två gånger per säsong tillsammans med en medlem.

### Ingår träning med tränare?

Träning med tränare på tisdagar och torsdagar ingår i avgiften.

Först när du har klarat singelprovet.

Dagens ansvarige bestämmer om båtarna får gå ut.

Vi deltar i tre regattor varje sommar.

Ja, gymmet är öppet året runt.

Båtarna är bara för medlemmar och kan inte hyras.

Boka i appen minst en timme i förväg.

Ja, det finns duschar och bastu i klubbhuset.

Privata båtar kan förvaras mot en avgift om det finns plats.

### Finns det skåp?

Ja, ett skåp kostar 100 kr per säsong.

Parkeringen bakom båthuset är gratis.

Mejla kassören före den 1 december.

Du kan pausa en säsong i taget.

### Vem driver klubben?

En styrelse som väljs på årsmötet i mars.

Anmäl dig till en arbetsdag i klubbkalendern.

# Vanliga frågor

### Hur blir jag medlem?

Fyll i formuläret på medlemssidan.

### Behöver jag kunna simma?

Ja, alla medlemmar måste kunna simma 200 meter.

### Finns det en åldersgräns?

Juniorer kan börja ro från 12 års ålder.

### När börjar säsongen?

Säsongen börjar i april, när isen har gått.

### Kan jag prova innan jag går med?

Ja, vi har prova-på-kvällar varje tisdag i maj.

### Vad ska jag ha på mig?

Åtsittande träningskläder som du kan röra dig i.

### Får jag en nyckel till båthuset?

Ja, depositionen för nyckeln är 100 kr.

### Får jag ta med en gäst?

Gäster får ro två gånger per säsong tillsammans med en medlem.

### Ingår träning med tränare?

Träning med tränare på tisdagar och torsdagar ingår i avgiften.

### Får jag ro ensam?

Först när du har klarat singelprovet.

### Vad händer vid dåligt väder?

Dagens ansvarige bestämmer om båtarna får gå ut.

### Tävlar ni?

Vi deltar i tre regattor varje sommar.

### Finns det ett gym?

Ja, gymmet är öppet året runt.

### Kan jag hyra en båt?

Båtarna är bara för medlemmar och kan inte hyras.

### Hur bokar jag en båt?

Boka i appen minst en timme i förväg.

### Finns det duschar?

Ja, det finns duschar och bastu i klubbhuset.

### Kan jag förvara min egen båt?

Privata båtar kan förvaras mot en avgift om det finns plats.

### Finns det skåp?

Ja, ett skåp kostar 100 kr per säsong.

### Finns det parkering?

Parkeringen bakom båthuset är gratis.

### Ordnar ni sociala aktiviteter?

Ja, vi har en vårfest och en höstmiddag.

### Hur säger jag upp mitt medlemskap?

Mejla kassören före den 1 december.

### Kan jag pausa mitt medlemskap?

Du kan pausa en säsong i taget.

### Vem driver klubben?

En styrelse som väljs på årsmötet i mars.

### Hur kan jag hjälpa till?

Anmäl dig till en arbetsdag i klubbkalendern.

### How do I become a member?

Fill in the form on the membership page.

### Do I need to know how to swim?

Yes, all members must be able to swim 200 metres.

### Is there an age limit?

Juniors can start rowing from the age of 12.

### When does the season start?

The season starts in April, when the ice has gone.

### Can I try before joining?

Yes, we hold try-out evenings every Tuesday in May.

### What should I wear?

Tight-fitting sports clothes that you can move in.

### Do I get a key to the boathouse?

Guests may row twice per season with a member.

### Is coaching included?

Coaching on Tuesdays and Thursdays is included in the fee.

### Can I row alone?

Only after passing the sculling test.

### What happens in bad weather?

The duty officer decides whether boats may go out.

### Do you race?

We enter three regattas each summer.

### Is there a gym?

Yes, the gym is open all year round.

### Can I rent a boat?

Boats are for members only and cannot be rented.

### How do I book a boat?

Book in the app at least one hour ahead.

### Are there showers?

Yes, there are showers and a sauna in the clubhouse.

### Can I store my own boat?

Private boats can be stored for a fee if there is room.

### Do you have lockers?

Yes, lockers cost 100 SEK per season.

### Is there parking?

Parking is free behind the boathouse.

### Do you organise social events?

Yes, we hold a spring party and an autumn dinner.

### How do I cancel my membership?

Email the treasurer before 1 December.

### Can I pause my membership?

You can pause for one season at a time.

### Who runs the club?

A board elected at the annual meeting in March.

### How can I help out?

Sign up for a work day on the club calendar.

# Vanliga frågor

### Hur blir jag medlem?

Fyll i formuläret på medlemssidan.

### Behöver jag kunna simma?

Ja, alla medlemmar måste kunna simma 200 meter.

### Finns det en åldersgräns?

Juniorer kan börja ro från 12 års ålder.

### När börjar säsongen?

Säsongen börjar i april, när isen har gått.

### Kan jag prova innan jag går med?

Ja, vi har prova-på-kvällar varje tisdag i maj.

### Vad ska jag ha på mig?

Åtsittande träningskläder som du kan röra dig i.

### Får jag en nyckel till båthuset?

Ja, depositionen för nyckeln är 100 kr.

### Får jag ta med en gäst?

Gäster får ro två gånger per säsong tillsammans med en medlem.

### Ingår träning med tränare?

Träning med tränare på tisdagar och torsdagar ingår i avgiften.

### Får jag ro ensam?

Först när du har klarat singelprovet.

### Vad händer vid dåligt väder?

Dagens ansvarige bestämmer om båtarna får gå ut.

### Tävlar ni?

Vi deltar i tre regattor varje sommar.

### Finns det ett gym?

Ja, gymmet är öppet året runt.

### Kan jag hyra en båt?

Båtarna är bara för medlemmar och kan inte hyras.

### Hur bokar jag en båt?

Boka i appen minst en timme i förväg.

### Finns det duschar?

Ja, det finns duschar och bastu i klubbhuset.

### Kan jag förvara min egen båt?

Privata båtar kan förvaras mot en avgift om det finns plats.

### Finns det skåp?

Ja, ett skåp kostar 100 kr per säsong.

### Finns det parkering?

Parkeringen bakom båthuset är gratis.

### Ordnar ni sociala aktiviteter?

Ja, vi har en vårfest och en höstmiddag.

### Hur säger jag upp mitt medlemskap?

Mejla kassören före den 1 december.

### Kan jag pausa mitt medlemskap?

Du kan pausa en säsong i taget.

### Vem driver klubben?

En styrelse som väljs på årsmötet i mars.

### Hur kan jag hjälpa till?

Anmäl dig till en arbetsdag i klubbkalendern.

Skicka e-post till styrelsen på board@riverside.example.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.

- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

The English file has no livestreaming feature row (`feat-5b0e7a13`). The only English mention of streaming is in the key features list: "live results, live streaming, a dedicated tournament website…". That is a short list of features and has nothing to do with payouts, so it needs no edit.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:

- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not.
